title: Three perfect days in Prague: the Old Town, Letná and Karlín
dek: The weekend before the big Christmas markets open: a Friday in the Old Town and Jewish quarter, a Saturday of galleries and market halls across the river, a Sunday on the hills above Karlín.

hero.caption: Old Town Square, a week before its Christmas market opens. Friday's walk crosses it at dusk.

intro:
Late November is a good time to see Prague. The leaves are down, the light goes before half past four, and the city moves indoors to its cafés, beer halls and concert halls. The big Christmas markets on Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square don't open until Saturday 28 November, so this weekend you get the Old Town without the crowds that come with them. The first market of the season does open on Friday 20 November on Náměstí Míru, in front of the Church of St. Ludmila.

The weekend's music is at the Rudolfinum, where the **Prague Sounds** festival closes its November run: jazz singer Samara Joy on Friday, Max Cooper's electronic set on Saturday and Anoushka Shankar on Sunday. Sparta play Liberec at Letná on Sunday evening, and Bohemians host Plzeň in Vršovice on Saturday.

This plan stays away from the castle side of the river, which was last weekend's guide. **Friday** is the Old Town and Josefov, timed for the Jewish Museum, which closes on Saturdays. **Saturday** crosses to Letná and Holešovice for the National Gallery's modern collection, DOX and dinner in the old slaughterhouse market halls. **Sunday** climbs from Karlín to the Vítkov memorial and the Žižkov TV tower, then comes back down for a brewery tap and dinner. Bring a warm coat and shoes that can handle wet cobbles. Most of the plan is indoors, and nearly every stop is a short tram ride from the next.

days.title: Friday: the Old Town and Josefov
days.intro: Breakfast under Art Nouveau chandeliers, the Jewish quarter while it's open, medieval altarpieces, then a Michelin dinner and Hrabal's pub.

stops.name: Kavárna Obecní dům
stops.text: The café in the **Municipal House** is the city's best room for breakfast: brass, mirrors, chandeliers and big windows onto Náměstí Republiky, all from 1912. Order coffee and something from the cake counter, or a full breakfast if you want one, and take your time. You'll see the building again if you go to a concert in Smetana Hall upstairs. It opens at 08:00 every day, so you can get in before the tour groups.

stops.name: Jewish Museum in Prague
stops.text: One ticket covers the Maisel, Pinkas, Klausen and Spanish synagogues and the Old Jewish Cemetery, where the gravestones lean against each other under the bare trees. The Pinkas Synagogue's walls carry the hand-painted names of almost 80,000 Bohemian and Moravian Jews killed in the Holocaust, and upstairs are children's drawings from Terezín. Friday is the day to go, because the museum closes on Saturdays. Winter hours are 09:00 to 16:30, and the Old-New Synagogue usually closes an hour before Shabbat begins. Buy tickets online.

stops.name: Lokál Dlouhááá
stops.text: A long, loud beer hall that runs on tank Pilsner and Czech pub cooking: goulash with dumplings, schnitzel, roast pork with cabbage. Locals come here as well as visitors, and the waiters keep the beer coming until you put a coaster on your glass. It opens at 11:00 and gets full at lunchtime on Fridays, so reserve a table online, or go for the counter and stand.

stops.name: Convent of St. Agnes
stops.text: Prague's oldest Gothic buildings, a convent from the 13th century, now hold the National Gallery's *Medieval Art in Bohemia and Central Europe 1200–1550*. Panel paintings and carved Madonnas from the age of Charles IV fill cool cloisters, and on a November afternoon you may have whole rooms to yourself. There's a touch display for blind visitors too. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00. Use the entrance on Anežská or Na Františku.

stops.name: Old Town Square and the Astronomical Clock
stops.text: Walk back through the lanes to Old Town Square as the light goes, around half past four this time of year, and the Týn Church towers are lit. Stand under the Astronomical Clock on the Old Town Hall for the hourly show of apostles and a rattling skeleton. The square's Christmas market and tree don't open until 28 November, so this is a rare quiet week. Then walk down Karlova to the river for Charles Bridge in the dark.

stops.name: Field
stops.text: Radek Kašpárek's Michelin-starred restaurant, a few steps from St. Agnes, is the special-occasion dinner of the weekend. Reserve as early as you can. Dinner runs 18:00 to 22:30, and if no table shows in the online form, the restaurant is full. If you have tickets for Samara Joy at the Rudolfinum (19:00), have Field for lunch instead, 11:00 to 14:30. Smart casual, and no children under six.

stops.name: U Zlatého tygra
stops.text: Bohumil Hrabal's pub. He held court at the back table by the kitchen door, and Václav Havel brought Bill Clinton here for a beer. Nothing much has changed. It's a plain Plzeň-style tap room full of regulars, with Pilsner poured fast. Open daily 15:00 to 23:00. Tables fill early, so be polite, ask before taking an empty chair, and don't mind sharing.

days.title: Saturday: Letná and Holešovice
days.intro: Across the river to the park above the bend, the National Gallery's modern collection, DOX, and an evening in the old slaughterhouse market.

stops.name: Eska Letná
stops.text: The Letná branch of Prague's best-known sourdough bakery is mostly a shop and coffee bar, which suits a quick breakfast before a long day. Get bread with butter and ham or cheese, or eggs, plus a pastry and a coffee, and buy a loaf of the rye Bread 33 for later. It opens at 09:00 on weekends, on the corner of Veletržní and Malířská, five minutes from Letná Park.

stops.name: Letná Park and the Metronome
stops.text: Walk south through Letná Park to the bluff above the Vltava, where the river bends under its bridges and the Old Town is laid out below you. The giant **Metronome** stands where the Stalin monument once was, before it was blown up in 1962. Skateboarders use the plinth now. In winter the park's outdoor ice rink opens. This season it opened on 14 November and runs 09:00 to 21:00 daily, if you want to skate.

stops.name: Trade Fair Palace (National Gallery)
stops.text: A functionalist exhibition hall from the 1920s, as big as a liner, now home to the National Gallery's modern and contemporary collection. Work your way up through the floors: the long 19th century, the First Republic between the wars, *Architecture for All* (1956–1989), then Czech art from 1939 to 2021. Kupka and the Czech Cubists are the high points. Allow two hours. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00.

stops.name: Naše maso Holešovice
stops.text: Walk east to the **Holešovice Market**, a city slaughterhouse built in the 1890s, whose brick halls are now full of food stalls and workshops. In Hall 27 the butcher Naše maso sells Czech beef and pork over the counter and cooks it too: burgers, sausages, steak tartare, meatloaf sandwiches. Eat standing at the counter or wherever you can find a seat. Open Saturday 09:00 to 20:00.

stops.name: DOX Centre for Contemporary Art
stops.text: Prague's big independent art space, in a converted factory a few streets from the market. This month it shows *Argus & Medusa: On Hope in Dark Times*, David Tibet's *Hallucinate, Children* and *ANDROS*, with the long-running *Point of View 4: Resilience*. Go up to *Gulliver*, the wooden airship parked on the roof, which works as a reading room. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 to 19:00, last tickets 30 minutes before close.

stops.name: Skô
stops.text: Back at the market, Hall 28 is Skô, a Slovak-leaning kitchen with some dishes cooked over an open fire. Order langoš, halušky or lokše, and whatever the fire is smoking that night, with a glass of draft wine from the cellar. The sausages, smoked ham and preserves are made in-house, and you can take some away. Open Monday to Saturday, 17:00 to 23:00, and closed Sundays, so tonight is the night. Book ahead.

stops.name: Cross Club
stops.text: A ten-minute walk north, past the tracks, is Cross Club, a club and café built out of welded scrap metal, pipes, gears and blinking machinery, with several floors and a courtyard. The café is open until 02:00 for a beer. On Saturdays the club runs until 07:00 and charges a small entry fee, with drum and bass, techno or live bands depending on the night. The 21 November line-up wasn't out when we checked, so look at the programme before you go.

days.title: Sunday: Karlín and Žižkov
days.intro: Breakfast in Karlín's old factory streets, then up Vítkov hill and the TV tower, and back down for beer and dinner.

stops.name: Eska Karlín
stops.text: The original Eska, in a converted factory, is a bakery, shop and modern Czech kitchen in one. Order a weekend breakfast of bread with cultured butter, eggs and seasonal small plates, and have a buchta or koláč with your coffee. It opens at 09:00 on Sundays and fills by ten, so arrive early. Karlín's wide, gridded streets are good for a short walk afterwards.

stops.name: National Memorial on Vítkov Hill
stops.text: Walk up the wooded side of Vítkov to the huge granite memorial and the equestrian statue of the Hussite general Jan Žižka, one of the largest bronze horsemen in the world. Inside are exhibitions on Czech and Czechoslovak statehood, the Art Deco ceremonial hall, and the mausoleum where communist leaders' bodies once lay. Climb to the roof terrace for the view. Entry is free. Open Sunday 10:00 to 18:00, last entry 17:30.

stops.name: Pho u paní Loan
stops.text: Prague has one of Europe's largest Vietnamese communities, and its pho places are some of the most reliable cheap lunches in the city. Mrs. Loan's small Karlín restaurant does pho, bún bò Nam Bộ, chicken pad Thai, spring rolls and plenty of vegetarian dishes. It's quick and good after a cold walk. Open Sunday 11:00 to 21:00. Walk back down the hill on the Karlín side to get there.

stops.name: Žižkov Television Tower
stops.text: Prague's strangest landmark, a concrete rocket from the 1980s with David Černý's giant faceless babies crawling up its legs. Lifts take about 38 seconds to reach the observation cabins, about 93 metres up, which have a 360-degree view over the city. On a clear afternoon you'll see the castle and the hills beyond. Adult tickets are 350 CZK. It's open daily 09:00 to midnight, so you can also go after dark. Tram 5, 9 or 15 to Lipanská.

stops.name: Dva Kohouti
stops.text: Back in Karlín, the Two Roosters is a courtyard brewery and taproom led by the Matuška brewing family, among the country's most admired craft brewers. Their beer is brewed on site: crisp lagers, hazy IPAs and seasonal specials. Try a small glass of two or three before you settle on one. It's busy with locals on Sunday evenings, which is the point. Open Sunday 12:00 to 22:00.

stops.name: Spojka Karlín
stops.text: An easy neighbourhood dining room for the last night. It grows vegetables and herbs in its own garden, buys organic meat from Czech farms, and bakes its own breads and desserts. Order seasonal plates to share, the meat of the day and a glass of wine. It's open until 23:00 on Sundays, which is late for Prague. Anoushka Shankar plays the Rudolfinum at 20:00 if you'd rather end with sitar. Karlín is four tram stops from the Old Town.

stay.name: Four Seasons Hotel Prague
stay.text: On the Vltava a few steps from Charles Bridge, with the castle across the water. You can walk to all of Friday's stops. The concierge arranges airport pickups.

stay.name: Hotel Josef
stay.text: A Design Hotels member on Rybná, with bright minimalist rooms by the architect Eva Jiřičná and glass-walled bathrooms. It's a short walk from Old Town Square and the Jewish Museum.

stay.name: Mama Shelter Prague
stay.text: A 238-room hotel on Veletržní, a few steps from the Trade Fair Palace. The lobby has games and a bar that locals use too. It's close to Saturday's stops and a tram ride from the Old Town.

events.name: Samara Joy at Prague Sounds
events.text: The Grammy-winning young jazz singer and a seven-piece band in Dvořák Hall, part of the Prague Sounds festival's Rudolfinum residency.

events.name: Christmas market on Náměstí Míru opens
events.text: Prague's first Christmas market of the season, in front of the Church of St. Ludmila. Open daily 10:00 to 20:00 with free entry. The Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square markets open 28 November.

events.name: Náplavka Farmers' Market
events.text: The Saturday riverside market of local produce, food and drink, on the embankment below Vyšehrad. Free entry.

events.name: Bohemians 1905 v Viktoria Plzeň
events.text: Chance Liga round 15 at the kangaroo club's small, loud home ground, against the league's western heavyweights.

events.name: Max Cooper at Prague Sounds
events.text: The electronic musician and visual artist brings his audiovisual show to the neo-Renaissance concert hall.

events.name: Sparta Prague v Slovan Liberec
events.text: Chance Liga round 15 at Sparta's stadium on Letná. Trams around Letná will be crowded before and after the match.

events.name: Anoushka Shankar at Prague Sounds
events.text: The sitar player and composer closes the Rudolfinum weekend of the festival.

know: From Václav Havel Airport (PRG), bus 59 runs to Nádraží Veleslavín on metro line A, about 35 minutes to the centre on a 46 CZK app ticket (50 CZK on paper). The AE Airport Express goes from Terminal 1 to the main railway station in about 45 minutes for 200 CZK. A taxi or ride-hail takes about 25 minutes.

On public transport, a 24-hour ticket costs 140 CZK in the PID Lítačka app (150 CZK on paper), and a 72-hour ticket 340 CZK (350 CZK). Activate app tickets at least a minute before boarding, and validate a paper ticket once, on first use. Trams and buses also take contactless cards.
The currency is the Czech koruna (CZK). Cards are taken almost everywhere. If a card terminal offers to charge you in your home currency, choose koruna.
Tipping: rounding up or adding about 10 percent for good service is normal. Tell the server the total you want to pay as you hand over your card, rather than leaving coins on the table.
Closures: the Jewish Museum is closed on Saturdays. The Trade Fair Palace, the Convent of St. Agnes and DOX are closed on Mondays. Skô is closed on Sundays.
It's dark by about 16:30, and late November is usually cold and grey, often with drizzle. Plan the walks for late morning and keep the afternoons indoors if it rains.

Sparta's home match on Sunday at 18:00 fills the trams around Letná. Bohemians play in Vršovice on Saturday at 18:00. The big Old Town and Wenceslas Square Christmas markets open on 28 November, not this weekend.
